title: The Strength of Hope and the Arithmetic of Regeneration
english: Those participating in the truth are as many truths as there are participants. I say these things before the end, for there will not be many truths, nor many people who are true, nor many experts, nor many knowings at the end; because if from the believing ones there comes 'one heart and one soul' (1 Sam 18:1) and 'being completed in the same mind and the same judgment' (Phil 2:2)—even if not from all, but rather according to a certain measure—at the final desired end, there will be no difference between one expert and another.

Just as, even if by hypothesis all doctors possessed medicine in an unsurpassed way in all its parts, there were not many doctors; there were many men, but not many doctors. Since therefore the truth is one—for 'grace and truth' (John 1:17) come 'through Jesus Christ'—one truth becomes through itself, not truths as individuals through it. They become through the one, just as partial virtues become through the universal and individual knowings through the universal.

Therefore the Lord seeks these; so strive as far as you are able to receive some truth, for God seeks these. Even if you receive [truth] regarding practical virtues, the truth of practical virtues is judged from the disposition, if one participates in justice through that very thing. Since 'let the righteous pursue justice rightly' (Ps 33:5), pursue that very justice rightly, pursue the practice of the righteous with a disposition of righteousness.

'Love the Lord, all you his saints' (Ps 5:7). He gave a reason; since 'the Lord seeks truth', 'love the Lord', the provider of truths. Thus we also hear righteousness being spoken of in the plural: 'The Lord is righteous and he loved righteousness' (Ps 116:15). But when he speaks concerning universal righteousness, the essence, 'righteousness descended from heaven' (Ps 11:7), he calls the Savior righteousness here. And just as it has become to us as wisdom, so also righteousness.

And they repay those who practice pride excessively. Since he showed the smallness of those who fear, for he also said there are men who trouble them, certain sophists and deceivers, he called these proud. But they practice pride excessively. And it is possible even thus: all evil becomes superfluous instead of being in vain. This indeed is also said in Proverbs: 'Do not love...'

against a man in vain; for even one hating a friend cannot do anything to him, unless God gives it. Therefore he does this in vain. And it is not necessary to strive for vain things. And these therefore the proud do pridefully in excess; for not all those of whom they boast will be subordinates to them, unless God gives it.

Be men, and let your heart be strong, all you who hope in the Lord (Psalm 31:6). Having said this, he anoints all the struggles for endurance, for manliness. And he does not speak of those who fear, but of those who hope. And we say that these are those working for the good of the promises with desire. These therefore are ready to become manly and to be strengthened and to draw near to God. And each one, clinging to Him, becomes one spirit with Him. And if each one of those clinging to the Lord becomes one with Him, when many are the ones clinging to Him, by a way of communion all become one spirit.

To David: of understanding. Blessed are those whose lawlessnesses have been forgiven (Psalm 32:1). The forgiveness of sins is a new genesis, a genesis upon genesis. Because of this it is called regeneration. Just as the repetition denotes song upon song, so also the regeneration is another genesis being added upon a genesis that has arrived. It was necessary, therefore, for the psalm concerning regeneration to have certain virtues in number. And from the fourth square, five times five takes an addition and receives the first of the perfect ones, the six; for the first of the perfect ones, having been added to the fourth of the squares, makes thirty-one. The five times five is a square. A square is that which is equal. These therefore, the numbers having been set forth, have become suitable to the regeneration; for it is necessary to have its constitution from a perfect number and from a square because of stability. The former genesis became corrupt. The first-formed ones turned away from perfect virtue and from the keeping of the divine commandment which they had received from God. It was necessary, therefore, for the second genesis to be more stable. The stable one has [its quality] from the square; it has the perfect one from the six, in the number being composed and partitioned from its own parts. And this must be said: even if the twenty-five is a square, it has its imperfection from sensible things; for the sensible things [are] five...

title: Understanding and the Nature of Gospel
english: the visible, the audible, the tasted, the smelled, the touched

to be among those being instructed. And since it seemed regarding him to be himself the teacher, it is necessary for the teacher to be helped by the students; having hidden it, he says: 'May God give you understanding in all things.' Therefore understanding is manifold; the word is homonymous, and it has many meanings.

And since he speaks about hidden things here, there lies that which is according to knowledge, that which is kindred to wisdom; for the psalm contains mysteries. And this must be said: it is impossible to understand grammatical words if one does not have understanding of letters, and it is not possible to understand the arguments of philosophers unless one has knowledge of their previously proposed thesis. So also the things of God are impossible to understand without divine understanding.

And why is it that grace is given to David alone, or the understanding is said to be from David? Observe that characteristics are known both from the giver and from the receiver, knowing them. For instance, even the Holy Spirit in the Scripture is called at times Elijah and at times John. Likewise also the Gospel is called at times of God, as of God giving and arranging it: 'set apart' for 'the gospel of God'; and at times from the one ministering it: for 'according to' 'my gospel'; and of those preaching, it is sometimes said they have received the gospel, and at times it is said as having been released: 'repent and believe in the gospel.' Such names, when they mean the same both with and without an addition—with a divine addition and without this, as I said, simply gospel and gospel of God—are the same. Therefore it is the same to say simply gospel and gospel of God. Thus, understanding is from the giving God, and from the prophet and his psalmist who received it, the understanding is said to be.

Blessed are they whose lawlessnesses have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered (Psalm 32:1). Sin differs from lawlessness. Lawlessness is the sinful practice of one not having law; for the transgressor of law is called lawless. 'Lawlessness reproaches a man' (1 John 3:4). And: 'The lawless man says that he sins in himself' (James 4:17). Even if in another way sin and lawlessness are the same: for this the divine John writes in the epistle concerning it: 'everyone who does sin and lawlessness does, and the...'

title: The distinction between active sin and the potential for evil
english: "Sin is lawlessness." If, therefore, one has sinned, he has in a certain way lawlessness; but he speaks of two things. For by a connective conjunction, he has shown that there are two. Then: "and sin is lawlessness." Sin is a genus of lawlessness; for he was saying that lawlessness is a species, when the one doing evil does not have law. And this is also called sin: the transgression or violation of the law, which I called lawlessness. It is like saying: "everyone having a horse has an animal"; the animal is a genus. Not everyone having an animal has a horse, but he having a horse has an animal. He who has the species has the genus. Thus also here he speaks, as if he were speaking of the same lawlessness and sin. But in thought there is a difference, because one is general and the other is in part; one is genus and the other is species; for he said that the name of sin lies both against transgression and against lawlessness.

Therefore both kinds sin: "for as many as sinned lawlessly" (Ps 51:2). Behold, these who are without law, they sin. "And as many as sinned in law": these are those having wisdom, having transgressions of the law. Both "sinned." But the forgiveness of lawlessness happens when the divine law, the spiritual one, the one "turning back souls," holds the lawless ones. Then the lawlessnesses are forgiven. And I say thus, the forgiveness of sins does not happen immediately. Jesus forgives if he says: "the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins" (Matt 9:6). And: "Child, your sins are forgiven" (Mark 2:5); for he does not say: "Behold, your sins have been forgiven I." He has given a power that is making new. And the energy having come to pass destroyed the evil. Therefore those whose sins were forgiven are blessed. Consequently, they return to the blameless law of God which turns back souls.

Thus the forgiveness of sins happens when the divine law according to the gospel comes; for this is the "spiritual law" by which souls are turned back, as I said. And those sins which come to pass through transgression of the law and are added, have a covering. The sins are covered. But it is impossible for those baptized once to again find the bath. They are covered through works of repentance. But you say that the sins, having been covered, are saved. Not "love," he says, "but...

Does it [love] remove a multitude of sins? For it does not utterly annihilate sins, but in another way; for he who performs works of love performs them. For no one who shows love toward a neighbor speaks against him, insults him, or acts unjustly. But when he does this, he lacks love toward him.

All these things are examined not as being currently active, not because they are hidden as if they were destined, but because the arriving love has hidden those things, that is, it has departed from them, it has cast them out. And if one must speak briefly, the arriving love stops the sin in its active state, leaving the potential for sin remaining. If anything is examined, it is the activity; for example, the repentant robber had sin in activity; he had repentance; the Savior gave him remission; the activities according to which he had lived were cast away. But the potentials remain, and they are examined.

For one must not pay attention to those who say that evil is a deprivation. There are some, and indeed a whole heresy of the Stoics, saying this: 'It is impossible for one who has cast away virtue to take it up again.' Just as it is impossible for one who has lost sensation to take it back, and therefore through this blindness and deafness are a deprivation, so they reason concerning virtue. But to us, who are simpler, and rather more unlearned, they say that there is no longer such a thing; for they say that there is no repentance after these things, no taking up of virtue again, but the evil remains for ever and brings appropriate punishment.

Therefore, sins are examined in the way I have said; they pass into potentiality; for it is blessed to have the potential for evil. Opposites do not coexist. He who has virtue in activity has the potential for evil, and this is a blessed thing. Therefore, one must not have virtue in potential, but in activity. For this reason also, God from the beginning, having made man 'in image and likeness' (Gen 1:26) of himself and 'upright,' just as the good was in potential, immediately also gave a law to prevent sin, so that sin might always remain in potential.
